lines.text: Detective Marcus here. Today's case: a tiny suspect, hiding in your drinking water.
This organism is a single cell with several flagella. So, is it a prokaryote, like a bacterium?
Look closer. It is bigger than a prokaryotic cell, and it has a nucleus. So it belongs to the domain Eukarya, the same domain as humans.
Its name is Giardia lamblia. It is a protist, and as a human parasite, it causes a diarrheal disease called giardiasis.
So what exactly is a protist? Protists are all the eukaryotes that are not plants, animals, or fungi.
That makes them a hugely diverse group. The name Protista was first used by Ernst Haeckel in 1866.
Scientists used to sort protists by what they resembled.
Animal like protozoa. Plant like protophyta, which are mostly algae. And fungus like slime molds and water molds.
But those groups were not based on real evolutionary relationships. Today, protists are classified using phylogenetics: grouping by evolutionary relatedness.
And it turns out many protists are not closely related at all. Almost every rule about them has a major exception.
A group full of exceptions. My favorite kind of case.
Today, protists are divided into four supergroups: Excavata, the SAR clade, Archaeplastida, and Unikonta.
In this lesson, we investigate the first two: Excavata, and the SAR clade.
Supergroup one: Excavata.
Excavates have an asymmetrical shape, with a feeding groove that looks excavated, or dug out, from one side of the cell.
They include parasites, photosynthetic species, and heterotrophic predators. Their subgroups are diplomonads, parabasalids, and euglenozoans.
First, the diplomonads. Most are parasites, including our suspect, Giardia.
Scientists once thought they had no mitochondria. But they do have tiny leftover mitochondria, called mitosomes, and their exact job is still not fully understood.
Diplomonads live where there is no oxygen, so they make energy through other pathways, such as glycolysis.
Each cell has two identical nuclei, and it swims using several flagella.
Next, the parabasalids. They also have reduced mitochondria.
In most organisms, mitochondria use oxygen to make energy. In parabasalids, they work without oxygen and release hydrogen gas, so they are called hydrogenosomes.
Parabasalids move using flagella, and a rippling membrane.
One example is Trichomonas vaginalis, which causes a sexually transmitted infection called trichomoniasis.

Men rarely show symptoms. Infected women may become more vulnerable to H I V, and to genital wart virus, which causes over ninety percent of cervical cancer. In pregnancy, it raises the risk of preterm delivery.
The third subgroup: euglenozoans. They include parasites, heterotrophs, autotrophs, and mixotrophs, from ten to five hundred micrometers long.
Euglenoids swim with two flagella, steering toward light that they sense with a simple eyespot.
Euglena is a mixotroph. In the light, it photosynthesizes. In the dark, its chloroplasts shrink and stop working, and it absorbs food from its surroundings instead.
Another euglenozoan group, the kinetoplastids, is named after the kinetoplast: a mass of D N A inside one single, oversized mitochondrion.
These include the trypanosomes. Trypanosoma brucei spends part of its life cycle inside the tsetse fly.
When a tsetse fly bites an infected person, the parasite grows in the fly's gut, then moves to its salivary glands. The next bite passes it to a new host.
Trypanosoma brucei causes African sleeping sickness in central Africa: severe fatigue, and then coma. Left untreated, it can be fatal.
Three Excavata suspects down. Now, the next lineup.
Supergroup two: the SAR clade. SAR stands for its three groups: Stramenopiles, Alveolates, and Rhizarians.

Each group has a signature. Stramenopiles have one hairy and one smooth flagellum. Alveolates have little sacs, called alveoli, under the plasma membrane. Rhizarians are amoebas with thin, threadlike pseudopodia.
Stramenopiles include diatoms, golden algae, and brown algae.
Their long front flagellum is covered in tiny three part bristles, called mastigonemes, which help push the cell forward.
Some stramenopiles are photosynthetic. Others are heterotrophs, including parasites like Blastocystis and the water molds, and gut partners like Opalina.
Next, the alveolates: dinoflagellates, apicomplexans, and ciliates. Most are single celled, but some form chains, and some cells reach millimeters long.
They feed in every way: parasitic, heterotrophic, autotrophic, and mixotrophic. Some even keep stolen chloroplasts from their prey.
Dinoflagellates are armored with plates of cellulose. Two flagella beat in grooves around the cell, so it spins as it swims. Dinos means whirling, and flagellum means whip.
Dinoflagellates are behind red tides, also called harmful algal blooms.
Apicomplexans are parasites that live inside animal tissues. At the tip of their infectious stage, the sporozoite, sits the apical complex, which helps them break into host cells.
Many need more than one host. Plasmodium, carried by mosquitoes, causes malaria.
Ciliates are covered in cilia. Cilia have the same structure as flagella, but they are shorter, far more numerous, and they beat in waves.
Finally, the rhizarians. Most are free living heterotrophs, and they are hard to grow in the lab.
A few became photosynthetic by taking in other organisms. Chlorarachniophytes took in a green alga, and Paulinella recently took in a cyanobacterium.
Forams and their relatives reach out with fine, threadlike pseudopods that can branch and join into nets.
Rhizarians matter in freshwater and soil. In some soils, cercozoans make up thirty to sixty percent of all protists.
Case summary.
Protists are eukaryotes that are not plants, animals, or fungi, now sorted by evolution into four supergroups.
Excavata: diplomonads, parabasalids, and euglenozoans. The SAR clade: stramenopiles, alveolates, and rhizarians.
From giardiasis and malaria to red tides and healthy soil, these tiny cells shape our health and our planet.
Case closed. Next time: Archaeplastida and Unikonta.
